title: Historical Machine Learning and Connectionism Reading Group
content: The reading group will explore the intellectual history of machine learning and artificial intelligence, tracing foundational ideas from early theories of neural computation and the perceptron through symbolic AI, the connectionist revival, deep learning, and contemporary foundation models.Rather than studying these methods only in their modern textbook form, we will return to the original papers, debates, and historical context in which they emerged. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The reading group will explore the intellectual history of machine learning and artificial intelligence, tracing foundational ideas from early theories of neural computation and the perceptron through symbolic AI, the connectionist revival, deep learning, and contemporary foundation models. Rather than studying these methods only in their modern textbook form, we will return to the original papers, debates, and historical context in which they emerged. Sessions will combine readings of foundational work by researchers such as McCulloch and Pitts, Rosenblatt, Minsky and Papert, Hopfield, Rumelhart, Hinton, and McClelland with occasional watch parties featuring archival documentaries, interviews, and television debates from the early history of AI. The group is intended for participants from across machine learning, cognitive science, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, and related fields. No prior background in the history of AI or connectionism is required; the goal is to understand not only how major ideas in machine learning work, but why they emerged, what problems they were intended to solve, and how earlier debates continue to shape AI research today.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Speaker: John Morrison, Professor of Philosophy, Barnard College Talk Abstract: It is often claimed that neural networks construct models of the world ("world models") and don't merely exploit heuristics. In this sense, they are said to understand their tasks. But it isn't always clear what having a world model amounts to, or what should count as evidence for or against. This talk has two parts. First, drawing on joint work with Raphaël Millière, I propose a minimal notion of a world model: a single, unified representation of a task that preserves its structural relations. I explain how this notion sits within a hierarchy of stronger ones, and argue that many disputes about world models are merely verbal. Second, drawing on joint work with collaborators at Columbia and NYU, I apply this framework to the standard example: Othello-GPT, a transformer trained to predict legal moves in Othello. I argue that the evidence is ambiguous once we adopt the right baselines (networks that plausibly use only heuristics) and the right metrics (which attend to patterns of error and the probabilities assigned to unchosen moves). I then introduce another kind of evidence that favors the heuristic interpretation: how quickly the network learns variants of Othello that extend rather than scramble the board's geometry. I end by drawing general lessons for attributing world models to neural networks, and by describing similar approaches for attributing algorithms and probabilistic inference.
summaryRaw: Do Neural Networks Have World Models?

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Attributing LLM outputs to the training examples that causally influence their behavior can give us visibility into LLMs’ opaque reasoning and help us understand subtle persona changes such as emergent misaligment. Unfortunately, finding training data attribution algorithms which are both accurate and scalable has remained an elusive goal. I argue for separately studying an Estimation Problem (accurately estimating the causal effect of a training example) and a Retrieval Problem (efficiently finding the highest-scoring training examples). I then present a generic retrieval method for influential sequences which can be paired with a wide range of influence estimators (including EKFAC) and for which one can obtain high confidence about recall. I discuss how causal training data attribution can be used as a tool to assure LLM alignment. Bio: Roger is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto, focusing on machine learning. Previously, he was a postdoc at the University of Toronto, after having received a Ph.D. at MIT, studying under Bill Freeman and Josh Tenenbaum. Before that, Roger did his undergraduate degree in symbolic systems and MS in computer science at Stanford University. Roger is a co-creator of Metacademy, a web site which uses a dependency graph of concepts to help you formulate personalized learning plans for machine learning and related topics.

location.name: PU Press Building (PAI, formally the AI Lab)

content: AI agents are changing research faster than any of us can keep up with alone. Someone in this building has likely already automated the literature review you dread or the figure pipeline you keep rebuilding, but these tricks rarely leave individual setups. This bi-weekly session is about changing that, so we stop reinventing workflows and start building on each other’s. The rule is simple: if you attend, you share. Bring one skill, workflow, or trick you created or adapted. No preparation expected, a casual 5-minute on-the-fly demo or explanation is plenty!

content: Hosted by Natural and Artificial Minds Speaker: Mel Andrews, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Center for Information Technology Policy and Natural and Artificial Minds Talk abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has sparked debate over the prospect of automating peer review in scientific publishing and funding allocation. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Hosted by Natural and Artificial Minds Speaker: Mel Andrews, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Center for Information Technology Policy and Natural and Artificial Minds Talk abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has sparked debate over the prospect of automating peer review in scientific publishing and funding allocation. Not all human tasks, however, are amenable to automation. The feasibility and even the conceptual coherence of automation depend on prior commitments to an account of peer review. Proposals for automated reviewing treat performance at the task of peer review as a benchmark, i.e., something that can be captured under quantitative, unitary, scalar, context-independent model evaluation practices. The benchmarking of review is revelatory of particular commitments to the nature of the task, which, taken together, we dub the measurement account of peer review. This account, we argue, is not epistemically coherent, and further, negates the social-epistemic nature of both scientific knowledge production and science evaluation. An eye to the historical development of peer reviewing practices reveals two compelling alternatives: the correspondence account and the democratic account of peer review. On these historically-backed accounts, peer review comes out resistant to attempts at automation. If peer review is indeed an irreducibly social-epistemic practice, offloading the task to LLMs or related technologies would not be an automation of peer review but rather a replacement of peer review with something wholly unlike it. This leaves open the question of whether peer review is a desirable institution to uphold in the context of modern science.
summaryRaw: Automated Social Epistemology: Language Models in Scientific Peer Review

title: Learning treatment effects and mechanisms in AI model evaluation
content: Hosted by Data-Driven Social Science Speaker: Apoorva Lal, Research Scientist, OpenAI Large language models offer new ways to improve both the precision and interpretation of randomized experiments, especially in settings where a model component (weights, sysprompts etc) itself is the randomized treatment. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Hosted by Data-Driven Social Science Speaker: Apoorva Lal, Research Scientist, OpenAI Large language models offer new ways to improve both the precision and interpretation of randomized experiments, especially in settings where a model component (weights, sysprompts etc) itself is the randomized treatment. The first paper studies AI-generated predictions as auxiliary covariates in standard regression adjustment and demonstrates that traditional regression machinery can be used fruitfully in conjunction with zero-shot or fine-tuned LLM predictions for precision gains, and appropriately calibrated adjustment has an asymptotic “do no harm” property when predictions are uninformative. The second paper proposes a complementary framework for investigating mechanisms expressed in text. LLM graders and/or embeddings would identify interpretable binary indicators, M_j, representing hypothesized mechanisms, with coding rules and predictive validity assessed on held-out data. We then propose estimators that plug these learned hypotheses into Baron–Kenny-style mediation regressions and complementary difference-in-differences regressions that compare treatment–control contrasts across settings with high versus low mechanism prevalence are consistent for learning effect mechanisms. Lunch will be provided.
summaryRaw: Learning treatment effects and mechanisms in AI model evaluation

title: NAM Chilloquium series: Mathematics in the age of AI
content: Speakers: Akshay Venkatesh, Institute for Advanced Study Arvind Narayanan, Computer Science and CITP AI systems are beginning to produce proofs for mathematical problems that researchers have worked on for decades. What do these developments tell us about the capabilities of AI, and how might they change the future of mathematics and scientific discovery? rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Speakers: Akshay Venkatesh, Institute for Advanced Study Arvind Narayanan, Computer Science and CITP AI systems are beginning to produce proofs for mathematical problems that researchers have worked on for decades. What do these developments tell us about the capabilities of AI, and how might they change the future of mathematics and scientific discovery? Join Professors Akshay Venkatesh (Institute for Advanced Study) and Arvind Narayanan (Computer Science, Princeton University) for an informal conversation about how AI is changing mathematical research, what it means to understand discoveries made by AI, and what researchers should focus on as these systems become increasingly capable. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Taming the Big Blob of Compute Abstractions let us study complex systems. In physics, Newtonian mechanics is wrong but useful for modeling physical systems at the right level of granularity. We use abstractions to study learning systems in the same way. As an example, I present a simple abstraction of how LLM loss depends on model size, data, and batch size. This abstraction is a noisy quadratic model of training that (partly) explains the Chinchilla scaling law and predicts LLM loss across a 1000x compute gap. Yet even this "successful" abstraction fails in certain critical regimes, and fixing it requires patching in LayerNorm-like effects. I argue this case is actually typical, because deep networks keep leaking through our abstractions. This leads me to a more radical proposal: rather than keep patching our abstractions, we should design model classes that admit them by construction, are easier to study by construction, all the while staying competitive with Transformers.
